title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Pacific Cod by Vessels Using Pot Gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska
summary:
The National Marine Fisheries Service has closed directed fishing for Pacific cod by boats using pot traps in the central Gulf of Alaska for the rest of 2025 to keep the harvest within this year’s catch limit. The closure took effect October 6 and runs through December 31, with a small amount of cod still allowed to be kept if caught incidentally while targeting other groundfish.

The agency moved quickly after new catch data showed the sector was at or near its annual share. Acting fast without the usual notice-and-comment period is meant to prevent overshooting the limit and to support long-term sustainability of the stock. In plain terms, this is a mid-season pause to avoid taking more cod than planned from this area and gear type.

Who benefits? The Pacific cod population and the broader marine ecosystem get a breather, which supports steadier fishing opportunities in future seasons. Fishing communities that rely on healthy, predictable stocks, consumers who value sustainable seafood, and other fisheries that may continue operating with bycatch safeguards in place also stand to gain from this precaution.

Who may be negatively affected? Skippers and crews who target cod with pot traps in the central Gulf of Alaska, along with processors, tender operators, and coastal businesses tied to that specific fishery, will likely see short-term revenue losses. Some boats may shift effort to other species or areas, but not all can do so easily or affordably. Depending on how supply adjusts, buyers and consumers could see tighter availability or higher prices for Pacific cod from this region in the near term.

Overall, this is a short-term closure aimed at protecting a long-term resource, balancing immediate economic impacts with the goal of keeping the fishery healthy and viable in the years ahead.
